pages.title: Languages of Odisha
pages.lead: A place is also made of the words people carry. Begin with Odia, then follow the other voices that make Odisha home.

sections.title: More than one way to belong

paragraphs.text: SCSTRTI’s learning catalogue includes Santali, Kui, Kuvi, Saora, Ho, Juang, Koya and other language-labelled resources. It offers a practical starting point for exploring Odisha’s linguistic diversity.
Here, each language will have room for its own stories, literature and everyday life. Odia is our primary focus; it is not the only voice in the collection.

A language, a script and a community are connected, but they are not interchangeable. We will preserve speakers’ names for their languages and explain differing classifications with sources. Regional voices such as Sambalpuri/Kosali and Desia are part of the research programme.
Have a family expression, a song title or a learning resource to share? Start with who uses it, where, and what it means to them.

pages.title: Odia
pages.lead: A language can be a page, a poem, a conversation—or the familiar sound that makes a distant place feel like home.

sections.title: A page that asks you to look closer

paragraphs.text: The photograph shows an Odia palm-leaf manuscript and a lekhani, or writing stylus, at Gyana Mandira library in Koraput. It is one surviving object to look at closely, not a date for the birth of the language.

The government’s literary overview places Sarala Das’s Mahabharata in the fifteenth century and describes later traditions of narrative and devotional verse. Its modern survey includes Radhanath Ray, Gangadhar Meher and Fakir Mohan Senapati, followed by further poetic movements and voices.
Follow a writer into a work, then return to the language with something new to listen for. Our literature collection begins that journey.

CIIL lists a 2019 introduction to Odia language, literature and culture, edited by Sanjaya Kumar Bag, intended for non-native learners. It is a useful bibliographic starting point; we have inspected its catalogue record, not the full book.
The next layer will add reviewed pronunciation, phrases and recordings by speakers. This first page makes no claim to be a complete history or a language course.

sections.title: Ol Chiki: a script with a story

paragraphs.text: The President’s Secretariat’s account of the 2026 centenary celebration credits Pandit Raghunath Murmu with creating Ol Chiki in 1925. It describes earlier use of Roman, Devanagari, Odia and Bengali scripts for Santali.
The age of a script is not the age of the language. Nor does one script represent every speaker’s writing practice.

Sahitya Akademi’s Santali award register lists Nalha, a poetry collection by Gobinda Chandra Majhi, as its 2016 winner. It gives a reader a particular author and work to seek out, beyond a general introduction to the script.
Start with an edition a fluent reader recommends. Ask what its title means in context, who is speaking in a poem, and what a translation carries—or leaves behind.

On 21 May 2022, Sahitya Akademi held a symposium in Baripada with the Santali department of MSCBD University. Its annual report names Damayanti Beshra among the scholars discussing Santali language, script and literature.
Read about Mayurbhanj with a literary question in mind: which writers are people reading now? The recorded symposium is part of the city’s cultural history, not an event available to book.
1925 · The President’s Secretariat credits Raghunath Murmu with inventing Ol Chiki in this year.
16 February 2026 · A centenary celebration in New Delhi recognised the script and contemporary Santali literary work. The event date and the 1925 origin date are separate milestones.

sections.title: Find your way into the words

paragraphs.text: You can begin with a writer, a work or a question. What makes us laugh? Who gets heard? What does a place remember? These are invitations to read, not a single interpretation of an entire tradition.
Sarala Das, Jagannath Das and Balaram Das offer starting points for exploring epic and devotional traditions. Later writers and poets open further paths through changing forms and concerns.
The collection will grow across poetry, fiction, drama, essays, translation and oral traditions. The names below are a first reading map, not a ranking.

pages.title: Fakir Mohan Senapati
pages.lead: Start with the everyday. Look again. A life that seems ordinary may hold a story about an entire society.

sections.title: A life in words and public work

paragraphs.text: Fakir Mohan Senapati (1843–1918) was born near Balasore. The University of California Press author note identifies his work as a poet, novelist, administrator and printer, among other roles.

The Government of Odisha’s profile highlights his humour and attention to common people and their difficulties. This is a useful entry into his prose: look for the people a grand account of history might pass by.
Six Acres and a Third follows the fortunes surrounding a plot of land in colonial Odisha. Read our short introduction, then follow the publisher’s edition details to choose a copy.
As you read, ask whose explanation you trust, who benefits from a transaction, and where humour changes the meaning of a scene. These are our reading prompts, not quotations from Senapati.

sections.title: Balasore: a place behind the pages

paragraphs.text: The publisher’s biography places Senapati’s birth near Balasore in 1843. It gives a starting point for a literary journey through the region, without turning a novelist’s imagined village into a verified map.

Before a visit, look for a locally recommended edition or a conversation with a bookseller. Ask which of his stories readers return to, and why. Museum access, memorial opening times and a walking route still need research.
1843–1918 · Senapati’s lifetime, as recorded by UC Press. His work crossed writing, administration and printing.
December 2005 · UC Press published the English paperback edition of Six Acres and a Third used in this introduction. This is a translation milestone, not the date of the original Odia work.

pages.title: Six Acres and a Third
pages.lead: A small piece of land can reveal a very large world.

paragraphs.text: Fakir Mohan Senapati’s novel is set in Odisha in the 1830s. A changing landholding brings property, law and village society into view; the publisher introduces it as a humorous account of colonial rural life.

The UC Press paperback lists Rabi Shankar Mishra, Satya Mohanty, Jatindra N. Nayak and Paul St.-Pierre as translators. Its publication date is December 2005, with ISBN 9780520228832. This is the translation edition date, not the original novel’s first publication.

sections.title: Take a question into the story

paragraphs.text: Who gets to describe what happened? What does owning land mean to different people? Where does a joke expose something serious? Keep those questions beside you as you read.

pages.title: Kui
pages.lead: A classroom, a short story, a language of home. Follow the words into everyday life.

sections.title: A language with its own place

paragraphs.text: CIIL classifies Kui as a South-Central Dravidian language spoken in Odisha and describes its relationship to Kuvi. This collection treats the two as separate languages.
A language name cannot tell you everything about a speaker. We will record locality and self-identification alongside each future contribution.
CIIL’s overview connects Kui with Kandhamal. The CIIL–NCERT primer credits teachers and contributors from places including Daringbadi, Balliguda and Tikabali.

Those credits make language work visible: people teach, review and prepare material for others to use. They are a useful starting point for learning, not a list of people offering visitor appointments.
ATLC’s catalogue lists Tahii, a Kui short-story collection by Anuj Mohan Pradhan, dated 2015. SCSTRTI also lists Kui supplementary readers and Pilanka Katha titles.
Begin with a title and ask a fluent reader how they would introduce it. The full stories, their settings and permissions still need review before we present excerpts.

The CIIL–NCERT Kui Primer dates its first edition to 9 March 2024. It introduces letters and basic numerals for early learners and adult literacy. The development credits include teachers from Kandhamal and Kui author Srikant Mallick.
A familiar word on a page can be a beginning. Open the primer with someone who reads Kui, then let their explanation lead the lesson.

paragraphs.text: CIIL uses Sora and also records Saora and Savara. It places the language in the South Munda group of the Austroasiatic family. We use Saora / Sora here while leaving room for speakers’ preferred names.
The CIIL overview locates speakers mainly in Gajapati, Rayagada and Ganjam in Odisha. These are broad connections, not exclusive language boundaries or a map of every community.

sections.title: More than one way to write

paragraphs.text: CIIL describes writing in Latin, Odia and Telugu scripts as well as Sorang Sompeng. It dates the latter’s creation to 1936 and associates its development with Malia Gomango and Mangei Gomango.
Script history and individual practice deserve careful listening. A letter chart cannot stand in for someone’s voice, faith or knowledge.
SCSTRTI’s catalogue offers Saora supplementary readers and Pilanka Katha titles.

For an oral story, preserve who told it, where, in which variety, and what permission they gave. A sacred or private narrative is not automatically material for a public encyclopedia. We will add reviewed recordings rather than simulate a speaker.

pages.title: Sarala Das
pages.lead: What happens when an epic enters the language of home? Start with Sarala Das, then follow the words.

paragraphs.text: The Government of Odisha’s literary overview places Sarala Das’s Mahabharata in the fifteenth century. Its discussion positions the work within the development of Odia literature.
An epic retelling invites a useful question: what does a familiar story become when readers meet it through another language and literary world?
The state’s Odia Classics catalogue provides a dedicated Sarala Mahabharata entry. It offers a primary route to the text collection rather than a modern synopsis alone.

Choose a section with an Odia reader. Compare a character’s choices or a remembered episode, keeping interpretation separate from the words on the page. This profile is not a completed comparison of editions.

This first profile uses the broad literary period, without assigning an unverified exact birth date. Stories of inspiration, manuscript history and differences between editions need separate sourcing before they become part of the narrative.

pages.title: Pratibha Ray
pages.lead: A familiar epic can change when another person gets to tell it. Enter through a woman’s questions, and keep reading.

sections.title: Writing and a life in education

paragraphs.text: In her own professional account, Pratibha Ray describes beginning as a school teacher, teaching in Odisha’s government colleges and retiring as a Professor of Education in 1998.
Sahitya Akademi’s author profile identifies Jajnaseni as Ray’s reconstruction of Draupadi’s life. Her own website provides an English excerpt under that title.
Try this reading question: whose choices move to the centre when a story is told through someone previously seen from the outside? The question is our invitation, not a quotation from the novel.

sections.title: Literature can bring a place into view

paragraphs.text: The Akademi profile connects Uttarmarg with the freedom fighters of Balikuda and Alabol, and discusses Shilapadma’s use of history and symbolism. These are literary connections, not verified filming locations.

Ray’s website records a stage-ballet adaptation of Jajnaseni by Hema Malini and screen adaptations of her work. This is an invitation to research those productions, not a claim that a performance or stream is currently available.

pages.title: Bhima Bhoi
pages.lead: A poem can begin as a prayer and grow into a question for the whole world: whose suffering do we notice?

paragraphs.text: Sahitya Akademi’s monograph by Sitakant Mahapatra reads Bhima Bhoi’s poetry through the Mahima faith and a powerful concern for human suffering. Compassion offers a starting point for approaching this nineteenth-century Odia poet.
Read slowly. Which lines address the divine, and which turn our attention back towards another person? This is an invitation to read, not a quotation from the poet.

Sambalpur district’s literary account lists Stuti Chintamani, Sruti Nisedha Gita, Ashtaka Bihari Gita and Bhajanamal among his works. The Akademi monograph offers a guided route into the writing and its interpretation.
Use a named edition and keep the translator’s credit beside any translation. Recordings and accurately checked Odia excerpts can deepen this page in a later editorial pass.

Mahapatra’s account connects Khaliapali with Bhima Bhoi’s later religious and literary activity. The photograph here shows a memorial setting, not the poet himself or a reconstruction of his lifetime.
Treat a future visit as a visit to a living place of devotion. Ask locally about access, observances and photography before going; we have not inspected visitor arrangements.

The monograph opens by noting uncertainty about his exact birth date, birthplace and the history of his blindness. This introduction leaves those questions open instead of selecting one account as certain.

pages.title: Gopinath Mohanty
pages.lead: A landscape holds more than a view. Follow a novelist into the lives, speech and unequal choices that give a place its human depth.

paragraphs.text: The author’s memorial website places his birth in Nagabali, Cuttack, in 1914. It describes an administrative career that began in 1938 and early work in Koraput, where he took an interest in local languages and lives.
Carry that connection as a reading question: how does someone’s work in a place shape what they notice—and what might their perspective leave out?

The memorial website describes Paraja through conflict between exploitation and those subjected to it, and credits Bikram Das with its English translation. Oxford University Press lists an English edition under Gopinath Mohanty’s name.
A novel is a crafted literary world. Read it alongside present-day voices from the communities concerned, rather than treating its characters as a guide to every person you meet.
The life sketch also names Amrutara Santana and Mati Matala among his major novels, and describes his interest in everyday speech, translation and language research.
Choose one work first. Note the edition and translator, then follow a recurring image, a conversation or a character’s decision through the book.
The memorial website includes interview and conversation links. They offer a listening route alongside the reading; the recordings remain with their hosts.
This profile uses biographical and publication records, not a completed reading of the novels. No invented quotation or unverified film adaptation is included.

pages.title: Ho
pages.lead: Listen for the words that make a gathering. Follow the words into everyday life.

paragraphs.text: SCSTRTI identifies Ho as Austroasiatic in its community profile, and names Mayurbhanj, Keonjhar and Angul among the Odisha locations associated with the community.
This is a starting point, not a complete map of speakers. Community identity, home language and the language someone uses at school or work need not be the same.

SCSTRTI’s account describes the akhara as a space for dance and the sarna as a sacred grove. These are cultural contexts recorded by the institute, not public attractions or a description of every Ho household.
What words belong to an ordinary day? Begin with a greeting, a place name or the name of something a speaker chooses to show you. Ask whether they want the word written down, and in which script.

pages.title: Juang
pages.lead: A house of memory. A language of its own. Follow the words into everyday life.

paragraphs.text: CIIL identifies Juang as a Munda language within the Austroasiatic family, spoken in parts of Keonjhar, Angul and Dhenkanal. Juang is the language’s name; Munda describes a wider language group.
This is a starting point, not a complete map of speakers. Community identity, home language and the language someone uses at school or work need not be the same.
CIIL also describes Juang being written in the Odia script. A shared writing system is a bridge for readers; it does not make the languages identical.

SCSTRTI describes the majang, also called mandaghar, as a community institution with roles in gatherings, music and shared resources. Its account also records an origin belief connecting ancestors to Rusi Tangar near Gonasika. This is a reported tradition, not an archaeological finding.

Begin with a story its teller wants to share. Ask how place names are pronounced, who taught the story and whether it is appropriate to publish. A public retelling should keep the teller’s context, credit and choice of words.

pages.title: Koya
pages.lead: Start with a season. Ask for the words around it. Follow the words into everyday life.

paragraphs.text: SCSTRTI identifies Koya as Dravidian in its community profile, and names Malkangiri among the Odisha locations associated with the community.
This is a starting point, not a complete map of speakers. Community identity, home language and the language someone uses at school or work need not be the same.

SCSTRTI’s Koya profile describes music and dance as part of festivals and gatherings. A published account is one starting point; the meaning of a song and whether it may be shared belong with its tellers.
A seasonal word can open a conversation about food, cultivation or memory. Let speakers choose what to explain. Do not assume a festival is open to visitors, or that a recording is yours to publish.

pages.title: Gangadhar Meher
pages.lead: A loom makes a world from threads. A poem makes one from words. Meet a poet whose life invites you to think about both kinds of making.
pages.identity_note: An editorial reading panel, not a portrait or quotation.

paragraphs.text: Sambalpur district’s account places Gangadhar Meher’s birth in Barpali, now in Bargarh district, in a weaving family. It remembers him under the name Swabhaba Kabi.

Hold craft and poetry together as a reading question. How does attention—to a line, a pattern, a rhythm—change what we notice? This comparison is our invitation, not a statement attributed to the poet.

sections.title: An old story can become a new poem

paragraphs.text: The Odisha government’s literary overview connects Meher’s themes to the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and other classical sources. His work offers a route into the continuing conversation between Odia poetry and epic narrative.

Sambalpur district lists Pranaya Ballari, Kichaka Badha and Indumati among his works. Ask a library or bookseller for a reliable edition of one title, with an introduction that explains its literary setting.

Choose a reliable edition with a named editor or translator. Follow one scene and ask what its sound, images and point of view make you feel. Keep a translation’s interpretation distinct from the original words.

sections.title: Follow the name back to a place

paragraphs.text: Barpali is a useful beginning for researching his life. A birthplace connection is not a promise that a house, memorial or library is currently open to visitors. Check arrangements locally before making a special trip.
If you know a local reading group, an accessible edition or an accurately credited recording, help us add that next layer. We have not yet selected an excerpt or recording for reproduction.

Try another Odia writer alongside Meher. What changes when a work addresses everyday lives, devotion or a familiar epic? Our profiles are starting points; the pleasure lies in returning to the writing itself.
